reliability_note: Same story as the Easytronic — automated single-clutch manual with lurchy, jerky, slow shifts and a noticeable pause on each change. Clutch and clutch-actuator wear are the common failures, and the actuator/electro-hydraulic unit itself can fail. Best avoided for stop-go driving.

Genuinely notorious. Automated single-clutch manual (robotised gearbox): slow, jerky, clunky shifts with a pronounced head-nod pause between gears, plus clutch-actuator and clutch wear that gets expensive. Poor low-speed and hill behaviour. A real reputation-killer in its day — avoid for a city buyer.

The problem child of this list. Mechatronic failures (early units had the synthetic oil in the mechatronic degrading, causing pressure/electrical faults; later it's the valve body/accumulator) plus dry-clutch judder and premature clutch wear — worst in stop-go city traffic, exactly your Bratislava DCT concern. Subject to warranty extensions in several markets.
Known trouble unit, dry-clutch again: clutch-actuator/mechatronic faults, low-speed jerkiness and judder in stop-go, and premature clutch wear. Warranty extensions in some markets.

The infamous one, and it earns it. This is the Getrag 6DCT250 dry dual-clutch (Fiesta/Focus/EcoSport). The core defect is the dry clutch and its control: violent shuddering and juddering on take-off, hesitation and lurching at low speed, and repeated TCM (transmission control module) failures. A second failure mode is the input-shaft seals weeping transmission fluid onto the clutch friction faces, which contaminates them and causes slip/shudder — clutches then need replacing at low mileage. It generated class-action lawsuits and buybacks in the US and Australia and is widely regarded as one of the worst mass-market transmissions ever fitted. For your advisory: a hard avoid for a city buyer, and any DPS6 car needs documented clutch/TCM history.

Sister to the 7-speed you already have, and mechanically a cousin of the DPS6 (both spring from the Getrag dry-PowerShift family). Same failure signature: dry-clutch judder and premature wear, jerky low-speed engagement in stop-go, and clutch-actuator/mechatronic faults. Better than the Ford in execution but the same architectural weakness.

The wet-clutch PowerShift (6DCT450), a different and far better unit than the dry DPS6. Much more durable, but still worth noting: some cars show low-speed shudder/judder and TCM or mechatronic faults, and it needs its fluid service respected. Nowhere near the DPS6's failure rate, but check for shudder and service history.
Much improved over the DQ200/DQ250 it replaced. Early cars had some low-speed juddering/hesitation resolved by software updates; no chronic mechanical failure pattern.

Classic weak point is the mechatronic/valve body (pressure-control faults → harsh shifts or lost gears), plus clutch-pack wear at high km. Reliable if the fluid + filter are changed roughly every 60k km; neglect is what kills them.
The strong DSG, built for AWD/high-torque and vans. Broadly reliable; occasional mechatronic issues but no chronic pattern.

The AMG GT / GT 4-door transaxle unit. Robust for a performance gearbox; the only real wear item is clutch-pack life under repeated launch-control starts and track abuse. No chronic road-use failure pattern.

PROVISIONAL — newer design with a limited track record, so treat fault data as provisional. Effectively no common fault for road use. Expensive to service, and repeated launch-control/track abuse eventually wears clutches, but the unit itself is exceptionally robust.

Based on the 9G-Tronic but with a wet start clutch replacing the torque converter (E63 W213, GT63 4-door). Robust; the start clutch can shudder or wear under hard repeated launches, but there's no chronic fault pattern in normal use.
